Formulation
- Predisposing factors: childhood asthma, history of severe exacerbation requiring intubation; allergic diathesis (hay fever, dust allergy)
- Precipitating factors: recent upper respiratory infection/cold leading to persistent cough and wheeze; missed/ran-out inhaler supply after being away at university
- Perpetuating factors: inconsistent inhaler availability/use, nonregular spacer use
- Protective factors: patient engaged with clinician, prior good response to inhalers, willingness to follow treatment plan and rest
- Summary: A patient with known asthma developed wheeze/cough after a recent cold while temporarily without inhaler supplies, leading to acute bronchospasm and anxiety about recurrence of prior severe exacerbation. Immediate plan focuses on restoring inhaler therapy, short oral steroid course, spacer provision, reassurance, and safety-netting.

Mental Health Care Plan Details

Principal Problem: Acute asthma exacerbation (wheeze, chest tightness, cough)
- Patient Goal(s):
  - Obtain and use inhaler therapy and spacer promptly
  - Reduce chest tightness and breathlessness; avoid hospitalization/intubation
- Clinical Goal(s):
  - Reverse bronchospasm and reduce airway inflammation
  - Prevent escalation requiring emergency care or admission
- Actions (Patient):
  - Fill and use prescribed Salbutamol (Ventolin) PRN as directed
  - Restart regular inhaled steroid (Clenil/Clenil Modulite) as prescribed
  - Use spacer with inhalers per instructions
  - Take oral steroid course as prescribed (two tablets each morning for five days; medication name not documented)
  - Rest and limit exertion until symptoms improve
  - Seek urgent medical attention if needing Salbutamol more frequently than every 3 hours, or if symptoms worsen (increasing shortness of breath, chest pain, light-headedness)
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Prescribed/arranged immediate supply of Salbutamol inhaler and Clenil Modulite inhaler (dose/administration details to be on prescriptions/labels)
  - Prescribed oral steroid course (two tablets in the morning for five days; drug name not documented)
  - Supplied/recommended spacer and usage instructions
  - Provided sick note/time off work advice (self-certify first 7 days)
  - Safety-netting advice and instructions on when to seek emergency care

Secondary Problem: Anxiety related to breathlessness and prior intubation
- Patient Goal(s):
  - Reduce fear and feel reassured while symptoms improve
  - Learn simple actions to manage symptoms and anxiety
- Clinical Goal(s):
  - Provide education and reassurance; monitor for worsening anxiety or respiratory distress
  - Ensure patient understands management plan and when to escalate care
- Actions (Patient):
  - Follow clinician advice: rest, take medications as prescribed, use spacer
  - Contact clinician/seek emergency care if symptoms escalate or if anxiety is uncontrollable
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Provide reassurance and clear verbal education about asthma management, spacer use, steroid side effects, and safety-netting
  - Advise to seek immediate medical care for worsening symptoms (e.g., increased breathlessness, frequent bronchodilator use, chest pain, light-headedness)
  - Offer follow-up if symptoms do not improve or anxiety persists (follow-up arrangement not documented — see review)

Patient Education, Emergency Care & Relapse Prevention
- Education Given: Yes. Topics Covered:
  - Nature of current asthma exacerbation and likely trigger (recent cold)
  - Use of Salbutamol as PRN reliever; threshold to seek care if used > every 3 hours
  - Use of Clenil Modulite as preventer inhaler
  - Use of spacer and brief instructions (priming puffs, inhale/exhale cycles)
  - Oral steroid course recommended; potential side effects discussed (mood change, raised blood sugar, rash, nausea, headache) and advised to read label
  - Safety-netting: seek further medical attention for worsening shortness of breath, chest pain, light-headedness
- Early Warning Signs of Relapse/Worsening:
  - Need for Salbutamol more frequently than every 3 hours
  - Increasing shortness of breath at rest or with minimal exertion
  - New chest pain, light-headedness, or other concerning deterioration
- Coping Strategies:
  - Rest and conserve energy
  - Use inhalers with spacer as instructed
  - Seek prompt medical assessment if symptoms worsen
  - Accept time off/work to recover (self-certify first seven days)
